answers.text: On click the start endpoint creates state, nonce and a PKCE verifier, saves them with mode, next and (for link) the user id in Redis at oauth:state:<state> with a 10 minute TTL, sets an oauth cookie holding state, and redirects to Google. 10 minutes matches the brief's round-trip limit.

The callback uses the state query value as the Redis key and also requires the oauth cookie to equal it, which ties the attempt to the browser. The entry is read and deleted at once. Missing, expired, reused or mismatched gives an error page and changes nothing.
It looks up the ID token's sub in user_identities.sub (unique). Email is never the key. Found means start_session for that user_id.

It only runs for an unlinked sub. It requires email_verified true, then matches the lowercased email against users.email. No match creates a passwordless verified user; a match leads to the password confirmation, or a refusal if that user already has a Google account.

The diagram was misleading and is redrawn. Straight to start_session happens only when a new user is created. Confirm password page happens only when a verified email matches an existing user without a Google account. A known sub goes to start_session earlier.

The pending link (user id and sub) is held in Redis at oauth:pending:<id> for 10 minutes, with the id in an HttpOnly cookie. Correct password: reset failed_logins, link, delete the pending link, start_session. Wrong: failed_logins plus 1 and the page shows again; at 5 the account locks for 15 minutes and the pending link is deleted. A locked account is rejected without checking the password.

start_session is the existing function in auth_flow.md: it deletes any old sid session, inserts a sessions row, sets the sid cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax) and redirects to next or /home. Uses the normal session means Google login calls it, with no new session type.

The mode (login or link) and the user id are stored in the Redis attempt at start, which for link requires a session. The callback reads the mode from there and checks the current session user equals the saved one. Unlinking a user with no password is refused with a message to set one via the existing reset email, which sets a password_hash.

questions.text: If the sub is already linked but that user's account is locked (locked_until in the future), does Google login still call start_session, or is the lockout checked?
Where does the `next` value saved in the attempt come from when the user clicks the Login button, and is it checked before redirecting to it after login?
After the callback, does the oauth cookie get cleared, and what does the browser hold from then on until start_session?
If Redis is down or fails when the callback reads and deletes the state entry, or when the pending link is saved, what does the user see?

When a new user is created from Google, what do the users row and user_identities row contain (email from the token, name, other required columns), and are both inserted together or can one fail alone?
questions.about: Create user: no password, verified email, link sub

questions.text: Which request submits the password on the confirm page (a new endpoint or the existing POST /login), and does it need anything besides the pending link cookie, such as the user typing their email?
If the session has expired or belongs to a different user by the time the callback runs in link mode, what exactly does the user see and is the attempt entry already gone?

answers.text: Lockout is not checked for a known sub. Lockout exists to stop password guessing, and Google has authenticated the user. The brief does not say either way, so it is listed under Open questions.

The start endpoint copies the next query parameter from the login page (if any) into the attempt. It is not checked there, because start_session already accepts only a relative path on our site and otherwise goes to /home. Now stated in Start and Terms.

Yes, the callback clears the oauth cookie once it has deleted the Redis entry. From then until start_session sets sid, the browser holds no Google-related cookie, except the pending link cookie in the confirm-password case.
If Redis fails on the callback read, or when saving a pending link, or at start, the user sees an error page and nothing changes. Simplest handling, no retry. Added to the steps and failure table.

The users row has the token email lowercased, password_hash null, email_verified_at now, and defaults for failed_logins, locked_until and created_at, per schema.sql. The schema has no name column, so no name is stored. The users and user_identities rows are inserted in one database transaction. If either fails, both roll back and an error page is shown.

A new endpoint, POST /auth/google/confirm, not the existing POST /login. It takes only the password; the user id comes from the pending link entry found through the cookie, so no email is typed. It reuses the lockout rules of POST /login.

The attempt entry is already deleted at the callback's first step, so the attempt cannot be reused. The user sees an error page and nothing changes; they start again from Settings (after signing in if needed). Added to Link mode and the failure table.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting point. A user on the login page clicks "Sign in with Google" (mode=login), or a logged-in user clicks "Link Google" in Settings (mode=link, which needs a session). Either way the browser requests GET /auth/google/start. The login page's `next` query parameter, if any, is copied into the attempt without checking.
2. Start endpoint. The server makes three random values: `state`, a nonce and a PKCE verifier. It saves an attempt record in Redis under `oauth:state:<state>` with a 10 minute TTL. The record holds the verifier, nonce, mode and `next`. In link mode it also holds the session user's id. It sets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax `oauth` cookie containing `state`. Then it redirects the browser to Google with the scopes `openid email profile`, the PKCE challenge, `state` and the nonce. If Redis fails here, the user sees an error page.
3. Google. The user authenticates at Google. Google redirects the browser to GET /auth/google/callback. The `state` comes back as a query value, along with a code or an error.
4. State check. The callback reads and deletes the Redis entry for `state` in a single step, so each attempt can be used once. It also requires the `oauth` cookie to equal the `state` query value, which ties the attempt to the browser that started it. The cookie is then cleared. If the entry is unknown, expired, already used or mismatched, or if Redis fails, the user sees an error page and nothing changes.
5. Google error. If Google sent an error, such as the user pressing Cancel, the user goes back to the login page or Settings (chosen by mode) with a neutral message. Nothing changes.
6. Code exchange. The server exchanges the code, sending the PKCE verifier. It checks the ID token's signature and nonce, then reads `sub`, `email` and `email_verified`. No Google tokens are kept. If this fails, the user sees an error page and nothing changes.
7. Branch on mode.
   - Link mode. The current session's user must equal the user saved in the attempt, or the user sees an error page. The attempt is already used up, so they must start again. If the `sub` is already linked to anyone, or the user already has a Google account, the user is refused back on Settings. Otherwise a `user_identities` row (user_id, sub) is inserted and the user returns to Settings. No password is asked, the emails need not match, and the session is unchanged.
   - Login mode, `sub` found in `user_identities`. The server calls `start_session(that user)`. Lockout is not checked.
   - Login mode, `sub` not found:
     - If `email_verified` is false, the user is refused and told to use email and password. Nothing is created.
     - If the lowercased verified email matches no user, one DB transaction creates the user (lowercased email, no password, `email_verified_at` now, other columns default) and its `user_identities` row. If either insert fails, both roll back and an error page is shown. On success the server calls `start_session`.
     - If the email matches a user who already has a Google account, the user is refused.
     - If the email matches a user without a Google account, the server saves a pending link in Redis under `oauth:pending:<id>`. It holds the user id and `sub`, with a 10 minute TTL, and the id goes in an HttpOnly cookie. The confirm password page is shown. If Redis fails, the user sees an error page and nothing changes.
8. Confirm password. The page posts only the password to POST /auth/google/confirm. The user is found through the pending-link cookie, so no email is typed. If the cookie or entry is missing or expired, the user goes back to the login page. If `locked_until` is in the future, the request is rejected without checking the password, and the pending link is deleted. A wrong password adds 1 to `failed_logins` and shows the page again. The fifth wrong password locks the account for 15 minutes, deletes the pending link and shows the locked message. A correct password resets `failed_logins`, inserts the `user_identities` row, deletes the pending link and calls `start_session`.
9. Ending a login. `start_session(user_id)` deletes any old `sid` session and inserts a `sessions` row. It sets the `sid` cookie and redirects to `next` if that is a relative path on the site, otherwise to `/home`. This is the same session mechanism as password login.
10. Unlink (Settings). This is allowed only if the user's `password_hash` is not null, and no password is asked. The server deletes the user's `user_identities` row. Otherwise the user is refused and told to set a password through the reset email (POST /forgot).
11. Notes. Accounts are matched by `sub`, so a changed Google email still reaches the same account. Google never changes `users.email`. Unique constraints on `sub` and `user_id` enforce one-to-one linking. A unique-constraint conflict or other insert failure (a race) gives an error page and no change. A password login for a user with no hash fails with the generic wrong-password message. The migration (the new table and nullable `password_hash`) must be deployed before the code.
gaps: The document does not say how the confirm-password POST proves the browser is the one that went through the Google flow, beyond the pending-link cookie. It does not say whether a CSRF token is needed.
The document does not say what link-mode attempts do if the user has no session at the start endpoint. It says Settings requires a session, but not what /auth/google/start does without one.

The document does not say what the existing lockout does to `failed_logins` after the lock expires, such as whether it resets to 0. It also does not say how a failed_logins count interacts with an account that is locked 'by this attempt'.

The document does not say what happens to the original `oauth` cookie and Redis attempt if the user abandons the flow at Google and never returns. The Redis entry simply expires, but the cookie lifetime is not given.

The document does not say what the confirm page does if the pending-link user was deleted, or if the `sub` or `user_id` became linked during the 10 minutes. It only says insert failures give an error page.
